question: Parliament has supported amending the rules to make it easier to suspend visa-free travel from countries that pose a threat to security or commit serious human rights violations1. The amended regulation will soon enter into force.

Venezuela, ruled by a regime that is hostile to us, with a penitentiary system in a state of collapse and ineffective public institutions, including health and psychiatric care, is a growing source of uncontrolled migration. Poland has already seen violent crimes committed by citizens of South American countries2.

At the same time, in Colombia and Mexico, we are once again witnessing alarming developments related to drug cartels and political violence. The Polish authorities have also broken up drug factories controlled by Latin American cartels3.

This comes as the United States is stepping up its fight against drug cartels and dangerous criminal groups, such as the Sinaloa Cartel, by classifying them as terrorist organisations4. In the face of increasing pressure, European authorities must be prepared for a possible influx of criminals seeking new sources of revenue and new areas of criminal activity.
EU statistics show that, despite the great geographical distance, it is citizens of Venezuela and Colombia who currently constitute the largest cohort of asylum seekers5. 1.
Does the Commission perceive in its analyses the growing problem of organised crime and migration from South America?
Is the Commission considering applying the mechanism provided for in the amended regulation to suspend visa-free travel from Venezuela and, if necessary, from other countries in Latin America?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.12.2025) The Commission closely monitors developments on migration and security in Latin America. Analysis confirms that certain criminal networks operating in the region have a transnational reach and can have an impact on the EU’s internal security1.

The Commission assesses organised crime and illegal migration challenges from that region in its regular risk assessments and addresses them in its cooperation with partner countries, as for example in the context of the EU-Latin American Committee on Internal Security (CLASI).

On 17 June 2025, the European Parliament and the Council reached the provisional political agreement on the revision of the visa suspension mechanism2, proposed by the Commission in October 2023. The revised visa suspension mechanism gives the EU a faster and more flexible tool to react and widens the grounds for suspension.

Every year the Commission adopts the visa suspension mechanism report, in which are assessed issues and risks in relation to visa-free countries. The next report will be adopted in December 2025. Activation of the mechanism depends on a thorough, evidence-based assessment in line with the Regulation3 and notifications by Member States.
